newsitem.title: PAPUA NEW GUINEA: PNG soldiers held hostage send Christmas message.
newsitem.headline: PNG soldiers held hostage send Christmas message.

text.p: PORT MORSEBY, Dec 23, Reuter - Five Papua New Guinea soldiers taken hostage by Bougainville secessionist rebels in September are safe and well and could be released next month, former prime minister Sir Michael Somare said on Monday.
Somare, who visited secessionist strongholds on Bougainville over the weekend, said rebels had given him an undertaking to release the soldiers in mid-January.
"The early release will show good faith on the part of the rebels," Somare said in a statement.
In a radio Christmas message on Monday one of the soldiers asked his family and relatives to pray for his early release.
"I want to tell my wife in Goroka and my girls that I am well and hopefully will be released soon," said another soldier in the message run by Australian Broadcasting Corporation (ABC).
In tears, each of the five hostages passed their greetings to their families from the back of a vehicle while rebels stood around them, said an ABC reporter who accompanied Somare.
The soldiers were taken hostage after rebels attacked the Kangu Beach government base in southern Bougainville, killing 11 soldiers.

Somare, who led this South Pacific nation to independence in 1975, travelled to Bougainville secretly after being invited by the Bougainville Revolutionary Army. He said the mission was a success, although the hostages were not released.
"We broke the ice and opened a new window of hope for meaningful dialogue to take place," Somare said.
"The government must begin negotiations with the rebels for peace and the restoration of (government) services," he said, adding that troops should be gradually withdrawn from Bougainville.
The eight-year secessionst rebellion on Bogainville, 800 km (500 miles) northeast of PNG capital Port Moresby, is the longest-running armed conflict in the South Pacific.
Numerous peace talks, some sponsored by Australia and the nearby Solomon Islands, and several major government military offensives have failed to resolve the conflict.
Hundreds of people have died in direct fighting or from disease through a lack of medical supplies reaching the island because of numerous government blockades.
